I got the priest to clear the way. Guess I'm ready to go now.
I hope you don't mind that I called an end to the funeral.
I'm sorry if I was too loud with those people. I don't know how well you knew them.
A maelstrom of emotions swells up as you approach the altar. Seeing his body up close is difficult in many ways.
(AMBITIOUS) None of these people cared. I want to make them leave.
(POWERFUL) I need some fresh air, but I can't even get out. It's like these people don't even try to listen.

[Look back at the crowd blocking the path]
The altar is lined on all sides by flowers, gifts, and letters of condolence. At the center, rising above everything else, lies the white-clad body of Clarence Bloodworth, your grandfather.
[Look at the letters and flowers]
[Look at the portrait]
[Whisper] Hey.
There's no answer. The sun begins to seep through the stained glass windows, and the altar almost appears like...a podium.
That's your spot, Grandpa. I can't take your place. No one can.
I..I'm not ready for that.
In the polished surface of the tiles beside the altar, you see your reflection. Tearful, pitiful. You can't help but feel small, and you don't like the sensation.
[Look away]
I look like shit.
...What would you do, grandpa?
As you glance back towards the crowds, your eye lands on a collection box by the side of the altar. Untouched, as if people are avoiding it.
So much for the spirit of giving, I suppose.
I'll drop a few loons in there on your behalf, Grandpa.
Wonder how the priest feels about that.
Really? You got here? Damn, something must have broken in the code.
Wait, really? Is this an easter egg? Should this happen?
His eyes are warm and gentle even in the now discolored picture. Almost instinctively, with concern, you search the crowd for signs of your father. He's not here.
[Step closer to the altar]
[Leave]
The emptiness of the altar emits a sense of energy, almost like it's beckoning you to fill the void. Maybe this is the way to go, after all.
Alright. Here goes nothing.
Okay. I'm ready for it.
[Take a deep breath and step up]
The murmurs and hushed conversations of the other attendees grows in volume.
I wish you could be here to help me.

...They might be a little bit more wary of his ire.
...They might listen to him.

[Step closer to the altar]
[Leave]
As you finish your speech, a flustered cacophony of voices begins to grow before fading out into the streets.
[Step down]
Some of them turn back to look at you, but you can't make out what they're saying. Are they talking about Clarence? Or you?
I'll be right back, Grandpa. I know what to do now.
I understand. I'll make them listen. All of them.
I'll show them what happens when you get in my way.
His face remains still and peaceful, but you get the feeling that your grandfather would approve of your little game.
[Leave]
Your eyes fixate on his. Even now, still and lifeless, they seem warm and reassuring. A faded presence of which you're just now becoming painfully aware.
[Step closer to the altar]
[Leave]
A draft slips past your feet. Was it always this cold in here?
I think you would've found it funny. He was real mad.
I don't really feel like going, though. Will you be okay?
I hope you don't mind. It's your funeral, after all.
You suddenly feel eyes on you, as if the entire room is staring. You turn, briefly, to look. No one returns your gaze.
I didn't recognize most of those people anyway.
How well did you know all these people?
I feel alone here without you.
As you speak, the voices behind you seem to swell. What starts of as a choir of exclamations, concerns, snide comments, and chit-chat coalesces into a cacophonous mess.
I wish they'd show you some respect.
Don't worry, Grandpa. I'll shut them up.
I lost my temper.
You approach the altar again, but you're met with nothing but silence. He really is gone. Maybe you should go, too.
[Leave]
There's that draft again. It can't have been this chilly in here all this time. Did someone open a door? A window?
I hope it's nice, wherever you are.
What should I do now, Grandpa?
...Grandpa?

I wish I could look at you again. The real you, not a picture.
Are they staring at me?
